NEW DELHI: Construction activities in Delhi will be completely banned from December 10 to January 20 as part of the government's measures to control air pollution during the winter season, chief minister Rekha Gupta said on Friday.In a post on X, Gupta urged people to report violations, saying construction sites measuring more than 500 square metres would be monitored through the Delhi government's Dust Portal and AI-enabled cameras.“Construction will be completely banned from 10 December to 20 January. If you spot any violation, inform MCD, your MLA, or me directly,” Gupta said.Gupta said construction had continued at some sites during the previous winter despite the implementation of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), with work being carried out behind covers.“Last time, even under GRAP, some construction continued behind covers,” she said.This year, such sites will be monitored in real time through the Dust Portal and AI-enabled cameras. Alerts generated by the system will be sent to the government's Control and Command Centre, Gupta said.“Notices, warnings and fines will follow,” she wrote, urging people to “inform, tag, complain and stop them”.The Delhi government launched Dust Portal 2.0 in July to strengthen monitoring of construction and demolition sites and improve enforcement of dust pollution-control measures.The portal, developed by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, integrates GIS mapping, live 360-degree PTZ cameras, PM10 and PM2.5 sensors and AI-based analytics to monitor compliance at construction sites measuring 500 square yards or more.The system generates yellow, orange and red alerts based on pollution levels and enables digital issuance of compliance certificates and enforcement notices when violations are detected.The upgraded portal also provides dashboards for district-wise monitoring, pollution trends and hotspot analysis.Officials and project proponents can remotely monitor construction sites through live camera feeds, sensor data and AI-generated analysis, according to news agency PTI.
Article Summary: Construction activities in Delhi will be completely banned from December 10 to January 20. Chief minister Rekha Gupta urged people to report violations. Construction sites measuring more than 500 square metres will be monitored through the Delhi government's Dust Portal and AI-enabled cameras.

Article Title: Chandigarh was built as a planned city. So why does it keep sinking in the rain?
Article Text:
Chandigarh's planned infrastructure faces recurring monsoon flooding issues

72.4mm and the city starts to sink

72.4 mm of rain brought Chandigarh's drainage system to a standstill

When roads in Chandigarh are no longer roads

Two-wheelers struggle amid severe waterlogging

A road literally washed away

A footpath caved

City’s drainage problem predates Tuesday rain

Reasons for Chandigarh getting flooded

It is not just a case of ‘too much rain’

Floodwaters entered shops

Planned city, unplanned outcome?

City was planned but the outcome is unplanned

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the Municipal Corporation invest more in upgrading the city drainage infrastructure? Definitely yes No, focus on maintenance instead 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Bridge damaged after heavy rain





CHANDIGARH: Chandigarh was designed to be different — a city of sectors, wide roads, planned green spaces and carefully engineered infrastructure.Yet, every monsoon, the same question returns: how can a city built around such meticulous planning repeatedly turn into a maze of flooded roads, stranded vehicles and submerged markets? Tuesday’s deluge offered another uncomfortable answer.A mere two hours of intense rain was enough to expose how vulnerable parts of the city have become.The city got 72.4mm of rain in just two hours, the heaviest two-hour downpour of the current monsoon season.What followed was something familiar but harder to ignore as an occasional monsoon quirk: roads turned into rivers, cars were stranded in waist-high water, houses and shops were flooded and thousands of commuters were stuck in traffic jams.The worst affected stretches were not in one corner of Chandigarh. Rapid water accumulation was reported in Sectors 17, 22, 24, 36, 37, 42 and 43, as well as along Jan Marg, Madhya Marg, Industrial Area Phases I and II, Hallomajra and areas around the Old Secretariat.Water seeped into corridors and basements of Sector 22, one of the busiest commercial centers of the city, flooded parking areas and shopkeepers had to resort to flex boards, mops and rags to keep water out.More troubling was the state of the city’s traffic network. Vehicles crawled through submerged stretches, bumper-to-bumper, two-wheelers struggled to negotiate potholes and hidden manholes and many cars broke down while trying to cross flooded junctions.Ambulances heading to PGIMER were reportedly stranded on Madhya Marg, showing how quickly a waterlogging problem can turn into an emergency-services crisis.Residents also complained about the poor management of traffic when it was most needed. Police personnel were said to be scarce on parts of Madhya Marg, including the stretch between Transport Light Point and the IAF Museum light point.Some places saw barricades coming up but commuters said there was little on-ground help to divert traffic or guide motorists through alternate routes. In a city where traffic was normally orderly, the lack of visible intervention became a problem in itself.The rain didn’t just flood roads, it wrecked one. A portion of the carriageway on Madhya Marg between Transport Light Point and Grain Market Chowk reportedly caved in or washed away, forcing the traffic police to divert traffic coming from Panchkula through the road behind Police Lines toward ITI Light Point.The incident pointed to another vulnerability, that of road infrastructure itself becoming the next victim if drainage systems fail.Downed trees and limbs also added to the disruption. Trees or branches had fallen on the roads in several places, including Sector 22, making the already congested carriageways narrower and posing additional hazards.It was not just that motorists would be late getting home. Residents said a badly clogged or blocked road can delay ambulances, fire trucks and other emergency vehicles when every second counts.Thus, the problem of Chandigarh is not that it rained. The problem is that known amounts of rain still result in predictable failures in known places.The Municipal Corporation undertakes cleaning and desilting of road gullies and storm water drains before the monsoon every year. But several waterlogging hotspots keep flooding.This means that cleaning alone cannot compensate for an aging or inadequate drainage network.The figures offer us a useful context. According to Central Ground Water Board data, Chandigarh receives an annual average rainfall of about 1,009.8mm, of which about 844.9mm falls during the monsoon.So, the city’s drainage infrastructure has to cope with serious seasonal rainfall, not freak events, as a basic design parameter.Another irony. In fact, Chandigarh had a rainfall deficit earlier in the monsoon. The city received 240.2mm till July 25, against the normal of 359.6mm for June-July, a deficit of around 33%.July itself had 200.9mm against a normal of 204mm. The lesson is a good one: a city doesn’t need a season’s worth of excess rain to flood. And a short furious spell can swamp the system if rain falls faster than the water can drain away.But the problem is no longer confined to Chandigarh. Residents across Mohali, Zirakpur, Kharar and Nayagaon were in the same familiar cycle on Tuesday.In Mohali’s Sector 70 and Phase 11, school buses, cars, two-wheelers and pedestrians were seen passing through stagnant water on waterlogged streets.Not only were flooded roads an inconvenience for children and elderly residents, they also increased the risk of slips and falls and exposure to unhygienic stagnant water.This is where the larger conversation on Chandigarh’s monsoon problem is needed. The city was planned, zoned and built with infrastructure in mind.But a city planned with infrastructure for an earlier era may become vulnerable when asked to cope with today’s rainfall intensity, traffic volumes, construction patterns and expanding urbanization. The thing is not that the drains were cleaned before the monsoon.The question that has become is whether the entire storm-water system still holds up for the city of Chandigarh.So the flooding on Tuesday should not end with water being pumped out, fallen trees cleared and the damaged carriageway repaired.These are essential emergency responses, but they are not a flood management strategy. The real test is whether the administration can identify all recurring hotspots, map drainage capacity against rainfall intensity, clear bottlenecks and redesign vulnerable stretches before the next cloudburst does the audit for it.Because the problem with Chandigarh is not that it has never been planned. It’s that the city has changed faster than some of the infrastructure under it.If 72.4mm of rain in two hours can bring Sector 17, Sector 22, Madhya Marg and several peripheral areas to a halt, the question for policymakers is not when will it rain again.How many more monsoons will it take for Chandigarh’s drainage system to catch up to the city it was meant to serve?
Article Summary: 72.4 mm of rain brought Chandigarh's drainage system to a standstill. The city got 72.4mm of rain in just two hours, the heaviest two-hour downpour of the current monsoon season. Roads turned into rivers, cars were stranded in waist- high water, houses and shops were flooded.

Article Title: Who is Gautam Rangarajan? Indian-origin strategist appointed to key role by UK PM Andy Burnham
Article Text:
Indian-origin strategist Gautam Rangarajan.

Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.
Article Summary: Gautam Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive. He has more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting. His appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.

Article Title: In 2020, Minnesota funded a $1.918 million Shell Rock River habitat program; by 2025, it had protected or restored 588 acres
Article Text:
Shell Rock River Watershed District (Image Credit: www.shellrock.org)

A habitat program takes shape

Three properties protected

Wetlands and prairie restored

More acres than planned

A longer-term conservation effort

In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. According to a 2025 final report from the Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council, the program ultimately protected, restored or enhanced 588 acres of habitat in the Shell Rock River watershed, exceeding its original goal of 483 acres.The funding was provided under Minnesota Laws 2020, with the appropriation directed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources for an agreement with the Shell Rock River Watershed District. The funding was intended to support land acquisition as well as the restoration and enhancement of aquatic habitat within the watershed. The program focused on several types of conservation work, including acquiring properties, restoring wetlands and improving aquatic habitat. The projects were selected using conservation planning and monitoring intended to identify areas where habitat improvements could provide significant benefits.The Shell Rock River Watershed is a shallow-lake system that supports fish, waterfowl and other wildlife. According to the final report, restoration projects were targeted at addressing habitat degradation and improving conditions for native fish, waterfowl and wildlife.One part of Phase IX involved acquiring three properties: the Glenville Property, the Bancroft Property, and the Church Lake Property. The District closed on the Glenville Property in March 2021 and the Bancroft Property in September 2021. For the Church Lake Property, the District transferred the deed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources in December 2024 after acquiring and restoring the parcel.The final report says these acquisitions contributed to the program's permanent protection of 218 acres. Another 370 acres of habitat and wetlands were enhanced or restored through the program. Together, those accomplishments contributed to the reported total of 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.The program included several restoration projects beyond property acquisition. The Bancroft Wetland Restoration was initiated in 2020, with construction beginning in June 2024 and largely completed by the fall of that year. Additional seeding work was completed in spring 2025. Another project focused on Panicum Prairie, where habitat enhancement work was carried out across 300 acres. The project involved native prairie vegetation and was substantially completed in February 2025, with final work completed in May.The program also supported the Fountain Lake In-Lake Habitat Project. Work included additional rock reefs and rock boulder clusters intended to improve fish habitat. The report notes that Phase IX funds were used to expand the scope of this work after the District determined additional funds were available. These projects addressed different parts of the watershed's ecosystem, from wetlands and prairie habitat to aquatic areas. The broader aim was to improve habitat conditions while protecting areas that could provide long-term benefits for wildlife.The program's original accomplishment plan called for 483 acres. By the end of the project, the final total had reached 588 acres, 105 acres more than initially planned. The report attributes the increase to the addition of the In-Lake Habitat Project and the Church Lake Property to Phase IX.According to the report, all grant funds were spent. The final grant expenditure remained $1.918 million, while the program's final total including leverage was $1.9479 million.The work is intended to continue beyond the end of the grant. The Shell Rock River Watershed District relies on multiple funding sources, including a local option sales tax, local levy and public funding, to maintain conservation projects. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will also maintain the Church Lake Property, which it owns.The program's results illustrate how a single state-funded conservation effort can combine land protection, wetland restoration, prairie enhancement and aquatic habitat improvements. Rather than focusing on one habitat type, Phase IX combined several projects across the Shell Rock River watershed. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored. The completed work represents a combination of permanent land protection and habitat improvements designed to support Minnesota's fish, waterfowl and wildlife over the long term.
Article Summary: In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.

Article Title: America’s top VC Chamath Palihapitiya may have just told Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: You have failed miserably; lists three ‘biggest mistakes’
Article Text:
Political fallout in the Ohio Senate race

Chamath Palihapitiya points to three things that are needed

Chamath Palihapitiya, a prominent venture capitalist and “All-In Podcast” co-host, has issued a warning to the leaders of top artificial intelligence (AI) labs, arguing that the technology sector is currently sitting on a dangerous ‘powder keg’ caused by mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. According to Palihapitiya, the executive leadership leading cutting-edge AI development has failed to persuade citizens of the sector's merits and the community-level value of hosting infrastructure facilities.“Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy,” Palihapitiya said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).Palihapitiya’s remarks came as a direct reaction to reporting from Axios revealing that the campaign branch for Senate Republicans sent a stern memo to prominent AI development organizations. The communication from the National Republican Senatorial Committee pointed out that data centres have turned into a fierce campaign vulnerability in Ohio, where former Senator Sherrod Brown is competing in a tight race against Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted.Husted is running to complete the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term.“Texas, Pennsylvania and now Ohio. This is a powder keg and has the potential to unwind 200-300 basis points of annual GDP if it metastasizes. How did it get this bad? The collective leadership of frontier AI has failed miserably in doing the basics,” he added.The committee noted that the two candidates are locked in a dead heat, warning that data centers represent the heaviest anchor dragging down Husted's campaign.To repair the widening trust deficit, Palihapitiya advised industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message rather than relying on technical jargon or stoking doomsday scenarios.1. Paint a positive picture of what is possible with AI. Instead of spilling the ink on the glass half full, stories abound of pearl clutching, catastrophizing or arcane technical jargon that, together, breed mistrust, fear and skepticism.2. Visibly and disproportionately enrich the local communities AI data centers operate in. Tell these stories with a megaphone and have local leaders lead with the financial proof so it’s irrefutable.3. Stop infighting and stop trying to influence the government or trick them because of the asymmetric knowledge the industry has relative to outsiders and observers. This further makes it seem like a shady money grab to many bystanders.He stressed that companies must clearly demonstrate the positive everyday possibilities enabled by AI.
Article Summary: Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya says AI sector is sitting on a dangerous 'powder keg' He points to mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. He advises industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message.

Article Title: Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra's 'reminder' to everyone investing in AI and calling it 'big': Right now, there is no AI without ...
Article Text:
Micron CEO feels AI is creating a more durable source

Demand outstripping supply

US chipmaker Micron reaches $1 trillion market capitalization

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra recently said that artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed the memory industry, long known for its boom-and-dust cycles. “Today there is no AI without memory. AI systems need more memory. They need higher performance memory. They need lower power memory,” Mehrotra told CNBC’s Jim Cramer on Mad Money. “So, the value of memory, that equation has totally changed.” His remarks came as Micron builds a vast semiconductor fabrication site near its Boise, Idaho headquarters, part of a planned $250 billion investment in U.S. manufacturing and research. The Boise complex will eventually house two fabs, each the size of 10 football fields, with the first expected to begin wafer production in mid‑2027.Mehrotra, who co‑founded SanDisk and has worked in chips for over 40 years, said AI is creating a more durable source of demand across data centers, autonomous vehicles, robots, and consumer devices. “Memory today is essential. That’s why I call it the strategic infrastructure of the AI era,” he said.Micron still cannot produce enough to meet demand. Mehrotra said data‑center customers want about 50% more supply than Micron can commit.The company has signed five‑year strategic agreements with 16 customers, with more added since its June earnings call, giving it greater visibility into long‑term demand. “All our customers across our end markets will buy everything that we make,” he said.In related news, recently, US chipmaker Micron Technology briefly crossed a market value of $1 trillion on May 26 as investor excitement around AI continued to drive demand for memory chips. According to a report by news agency Reuters, the sharp rally made Micron one of the biggest winners of the AI boom, with its shares rising more than 17% during trading. Micron’s stock jumped after brokerage UBS raised its price target on the company to $1,625 from $535, the report said. The company’s shares rose as much as 19.3% during the session before easing slightly later.As cited in the Reuters report, analysts say the surge reflects growing demand for advanced memory chips used in AI data centers and cloud infrastructure. The company’s rise also highlights how investors are now focusing beyond graphics chipmakers and looking at firms supplying key AI hardware components. “The need for pure memory has increased rapidly over very short periods of time, and clearly, Micron sits at the center of it,” Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth, told Reuters. “Today's crossing of the $1 trillion mark for Micron is just an exclamation point on the story of the massive amount of demand needed to run data centers in this AI revolution,” he added.
Article Summary: US chipmaker Micron reaches $1 trillion market capitalization. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra says AI is creating a more durable source of demand. Micron still cannot produce enough to meet demand for memory chips, MehroTra says. The company has signed five‑year strategic agreements with 16 customers.
